title: Generators, trimming and AOT
sub: Code at compile time instead of reflection at run time
cards/0/title: What is wrong with reflection at startup
cards/0/body:
A reflection-based serializer, DI container or logger does its work on every launch: it walks properties, reads attributes, compiles delegates. That costs startup time and memory. And nobody but the runtime sees that code: not the compiler, not the tool that strips unused code.

A source generator moves that work to compile time. It is a Roslyn component: it runs inside the project build, sees syntax and types, and adds new C# files. It cannot change existing code — so generators work through partial classes and partial methods: you declare, the generator writes the body.
cards/0/deep:
Generators arrived in .NET 5 (C# 9), and .NET 6 brought incremental ones (IIncrementalGenerator): the IDE reruns only the part whose inputs changed. Generated files show up in Solution Explorer under Dependencies → Analyzers, and with <EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles>true</EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles> they are written to disk under obj.

A generator sees attributes as symbols (AttributeData): the arguments from the blob, without creating an object and without running your code.
cards/1/q: What can a source generator do?
cards/1/options/0: Add new C# files to the compilation
cards/1/options/1: Change the body of an existing method
cards/1/options/3: Create an attribute object through GetCustomAttribute
cards/1/explain: A generator only adds code, and only during compilation. To plug into your type it needs partial: you write the declaration, the generator writes the implementation. It reads attributes as compiler metadata, not as objects.
cards/1/wrong/1: Existing code is read-only for a generator. That is why every .NET generator requires partial.
cards/2/title: System.Text.Json: a context instead of analysing the type
cards/2/body:
Without hints, JsonSerializer walks a type's properties with reflection the first time it meets the type, builds metadata and caches it. The first call is noticeably more expensive than the rest.

With the generator you declare a partial class derived from JsonSerializerContext and list the types with [JsonSerializable] attributes. The generator writes a ready JsonTypeInfo<T> for each: the property list, getters and setters as plain code. Pass it to Serialize — no reflection.
cards/2/deep:
The System.Text.Json generator arrived in .NET 6. Modes: metadata — generates a description of the type and the serializer works from it; serialization (fast path) — generates direct code writing to Utf8JsonWriter, serialization only. Choose with [JsonSourceGenerationOptions(GenerationMode = …)].

Since .NET 8 there is a project property JsonSerializerIsReflectionEnabledByDefault=false: serialization without a context throws InvalidOperationException with a clear message. That way a forgotten call shows up in normal debugging, not after publishing with AOT.
cards/3/q: Hook up the System.Text.Json generator for Order
cards/3/explain: Types are listed with [JsonSerializable], and the class must be partial so the generator can extend it. The ready context instance is the static Default property, with one JsonTypeInfo property per type. [Serializable] is a pseudo-attribute of the old serialization; the generator ignores it.
cards/4/title: Regex and logging: the same trick
cards/4/body:
new Regex(p, RegexOptions.Compiled) parses the pattern at run time and generates IL through Reflection.Emit — expensive at startup. [GeneratedRegex] (.NET 7) writes C# matching code at compile time: startup is free, and you can read the generated code and step through it in the debugger.

logger.LogInformation("Order {Id} paid", id) parses the template on every call (with a cache), boxes id into a params object[] and allocates the array — even when the level is disabled. [LoggerMessage] (.NET 6) generates a strongly typed method: an IsEnabled check, no array, no boxing.
cards/4/deep:
With C# 13 and .NET 9 [GeneratedRegex] can also go on a partial property: public static partial Regex IsoDate { get; }.

Where code cannot be generated at run time, RegexOptions.Compiled is silently ignored and the interpreter runs. [GeneratedRegex] has no such drop.

Other generators from .NET 8: configuration binding (EnableConfigurationBindingGenerator), options validation, the Request Delegate Generator for Minimal APIs.
cards/5/q: Match the tool with the work it removes from run time
cards/5/pairs/0/1: Walking the type's properties on the first Serialize
cards/5/pairs/2/1: params object[] and boxing on every call
cards/6/body:
Trimming removes, at publish time, code that static analysis cannot reach. Analysis does not see a call by string: the method may be removed, and at run time you get MissingMethodException or null from GetMethod.

Native AOT compiles the whole program to machine code ahead of time and always trims. There is no JIT at run time — so no Reflection.Emit, and a generic built through MakeGenericType may have no ready machine code. Reflection itself works — for whatever was kept.

The analyzer flags risky spots with warnings: IL2xxx for trimming, IL3xxx for AOT. Turn them on with <IsAotCompatible>true</IsAotCompatible> in a library or PublishAot in an app.
cards/6/deep:
IL2026 is a call to a member with [RequiresUnreferencedCode], IL3050 — with [RequiresDynamicCode]. In .NET 8+ these mark the APIs that cannot work without reflection over unknown types or code generation. Mark your own such method with the same attributes — the warning moves to its callers.

[UnconditionalSuppressMessage] silences a warning for good, including at publish time. Use it only once you have proven the needed members will be kept.
cards/7/q: What produces an analyzer warning with PublishAot? Select all.
cards/7/options/4: Type.GetType(name), where name is read from a file
cards/7/explain: Serialize without a context is marked RequiresUnreferencedCode and RequiresDynamicCode (IL2026, IL3050), DynamicMethod is RequiresDynamicCode (IL3050), an unknown string in Type.GetType is IL2057. But the analyzer understands typeof plus a constant string: the Calc method will be kept.
cards/8/title: DynamicallyAccessedMembers: a contract about what to keep
cards/8/body:
When a method takes a Type and does something with it through reflection, the analyzer does not know which members to keep. A [DynamicallyAccessedMembers] annotation on the parameter says: "this type needs its public constructors" (or methods, properties…).

The requirement flows up the call chain. A caller that passes typeof(Order) — the analyzer keeps what is needed. A caller passing its own Type parameter must annotate it too. And if at the top the type came from a string — that is where the warning lands.
cards/9/q: On which line does the trimming analyzer warn?
cards/9/explain: Inside Run everything is clean: the parameter is annotated, so GetMethod is allowed. The analyzer sees typeof(Job) and keeps Job's public methods — through a local variable too. But a type from a typed-in string is unknown: IL2057 on the last line.
cards/10/body:
In .NET Framework reflection was the norm: XmlSerializer generated assemblies at run time, BinaryFormatter wrote any object through reflection, DI containers scanned assemblies, and RegexOptions.Compiled generated IL. The JIT was always there; trimming was not.

Today the .NET libraries are annotated for trimming and AOT, and hot paths move to generators. BinaryFormatter was removed in .NET 9: its methods throw PlatformNotSupportedException.

The rule: reflection over known types at startup or in tools is fine. On a hot path — a delegate, UnsafeAccessor or a generator. Under AOT — a generator.
cards/11/q: At startup a mini-framework finds every class with [Handler] via Assembly.GetTypes() and creates them through Activator. The app must be published with Native AOT. What is best?
cards/11/options/0: A generator: build the handler list and their creation code at compile time
cards/11/options/3: Cache the found types in a static field
cards/11/explain: Trimming removes classes nothing references in code, and GetTypes simply does not return them — silently, with no error. A generator finds [Handler] at compile time and writes new HandlerA(), new HandlerB(): the analyzer sees direct references, and there is no reflection at run time.
cards/11/wrong/1: The warning goes away, the problem stays: removed classes are not found at run time.
cards/11/wrong/3: A cache speeds up repeated lookups but does not bring back removed types.
